speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words at third reading stage of this bill. We as members of Parliament usually say that we are pleased to speak on any piece of legislation. However, this concerns an area I have felt strongly about and I am very proud of the fact that I was able to be a part of the legislative committee and be one of the speakers on this.
In that context I want to thank the hon. member for Terrebonne who chaired the legislative committee that looked into this bill. Indeed, I thank all members of the legislative committee as well as officials from the Department of Justice. Through their work and their initiatives in the department, I think they are making a contribution to the quality of life in this country and they are making a difference by helping to solve a very difficult problem.
That difficult problem involves what happens when a couple becomes separated or divorced. This particular piece of legislation amends the Divorce Act as well as the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act. It involves amendments to both those acts. They are both steps in the right direction.
One thing that cannot help but strike anyone who started to study the law of this country, as I did 18 years ago, is that there are considerable problems with the whole question of support, particularly the support of children. The law as I understood it and as I experienced it in the relatively short period of time I practised law, made it extremely difficult for an individual to enforce a support order, in most cases against an estranged husband.
There were hundreds of thousands of examples over the years in which women particularly have suffered. Just as important, of course, our children suffer because their estranged father who does not have custody is not paying for support. That is wrong. That is fundamentally wrong.
No system of law in this country or in any other should in any way facilitate or not come to the assistance of children whose mother's counsel has obtained a support order. This is wrong. Nobody has the right it seems to me
Government Orders
to bring children into this world and then renege on their obligations to those children.
This sort of thing has gone on in this country for many, many years. Indeed, I remember seeing statistics in my province of Ontario that I am sure are mirrored across the country. Individuals who were up to date in their support payments of their children were the exception to the general rule. Normally support payments and schedules were not adhered to.
That is wrong and it seems to me that every legislator, everyone involved with the judicial system of this or any other country, has an obligation to change that, to do something about it. The problems do not involve just non-payment but what happens when circumstances change.
I can remember one particular example from when I practised law. A woman came in who had a provincial court support order in favour of her children. She told me her separated husband was not paying for the support of the children and that he had moved from Ontario to Manitoba.
The first thing that would go through a lawyer's head is good luck in trying to enforce a provincial court order from the province of Ontario if that individual has moved to another province.
It is not to say that there was not a procedure. There was a procedure. I am going by memory now about registering the provincial order in a superior court, having it transferred to a superior court in another province and then going through the enforcement procedures. It was a very long and expensive process for an individual to get justice and the support that the law requires, in that particular case, for her husband to pay.
One of the things that I was very pleased about after I became a member of Parliament was that the government did come forward with the Family Orders and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act. It was a step in the right direction.
I know just as we have passed this piece of legislation and as we did the previous one, the knock will always be "you should have done this last year" or "you should have gone farther". I am the first one to say that this does not solve all the problems of the enforcement of custody and changes to orders under the Divorce Act.

February 12, 1993
Government Orders
I agree with that. I agree it does not fix all the problems but it is a step in the right direction. This is a good piece of legislation just as the previous one was. It did not get much publicity. I used to talk about it. When people would say what are you doing in the justice area, I always told them that we are making it possible, that we are getting the federal government to co-operate with provincial authorities to get involved with collecting support payments from individuals who are under an obligation, not just legal but moral, to support their children.
I was very, very proud that the federal government was involved with that. I am very proud and pleased about this particular piece of legislation. This too is a step in the right direction. It helps in the enforcement of support orders by making some refinements, clearing up some of the red tape and responding to some of the problems we found in the last few years with the original piece of legislation.
As well, it helps individuals who have obtained a divorce and then, for whatever reasons, circumstances change and they want to make a change to the original order. This gives them some flexibility in terms of where they can go to get that changed. That too is a good idea and a step in the right direction but the process is not complete.
I know that the officials from the Department of Justice I referred to earlier are in discussion with their provincial counterparts. They are working on guidelines to help bring some consistency across Canada as to what, under certain circumstances, an individual, a child might expect in a support and custody hearing. I hope to see those recommendations later on this year, which is good.
There has been progress in this area. This is a step in the right direction. There is going to be more progress in this and that is good. I should add that we have seen progress at the provincial level. I do not mind saying that. I do not know what if anything the New Democrat Party in Ontario has done that I agree with, but I certainly agree with some of the moves that have been made in this particular area because this for too long has been a neglected area in society. I have made the comment and I believe it to be true.
If for the last 125 years our system of law and government had been dominated by women, this would
not be a problem and we would not need this legislation. This problem would have long since been cleared up.
I am proud to be part of an administration that believes this is a priority and is bringing it forward. I appreciate those individuals who came before the legislative committee. Indeed, I wish there had been more. We sent out invitations and we would have liked to have heard from more groups on this subject, but those individuals who did come forward did contribute positively to the debate.
One of the ideas that came forward was the whole question of taxation of support payments. That is obviously outside the scope of this particular piece of legislation but nonetheless an interesting proposal did come from one of the groups. The interesting proposal from this group was that we should remove the tax consideration of support payments in the hands of the payer and the payee. Generally in a support order the payee is in a higher tax bracket so the tax deduction is usually more valuable to him than the recipient so in effect there is a public subsidy to the whole question.
I am happily married to my wife. I have three children. I do not get a tax deduction. Certainly under the changes to legislation, it is a reasonable question to ask whether those who are separated should get a tax deduction for what otherwise is their moral obligation to look after their children.
I do not want to take up too much time but I hope that is a question that this House will consider. I agree it is beyond the scope of this bill but, as I say, it does touch on this whole area.
This is a step in the right direction and I look forward to the results of the discussions that departmental officials are having now with our provincial counterparts because I believe that too will be fruitful and helpful in this area.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be part of this debate on Bill C-79.
To follow what the parliamentary secretary has said, this is a bill to amend the Divorce Act and the Family Order and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act. Its goal is to improve the effectiveness in the support payment system. We are also supposedly improving the tracing and garnishment system of support payments.
February 12, 1993

With respect to the Divorce Act, the major change in the Divorce Act appears to be the simplification of the law so that it will be easier for former spouses living in different provinces to apply for custody or a support order.
With respect to the Family Order and Agreements Enforcement Assistance Act this will also reduce costs, this time for investigating child abduction. The proposed amendments remove the requirement that police officers get court authorization to use general federal data banks for tracing individuals in cases of spousal child abduction.
The witnesses who came before the legislative committee were of the opinion that this bill was a step forward. However, they felt that the whole process needed to go a lot further than was the case under these amendments. The problems that exist in the maintenance of children of parents who are separated or divorced is just not satisfactory and in fact is totally unacceptable.
We have a large number of children at risk who are not receiving the support that their single mothers can give and that is really no fault of the single mothers. To give an example, in a study of broken marriages by Statistics Canada which was done in June of last year men who paid alimony and child support had incomes more than twice as much as their partners who were looking after the children.
It is quite a shocking statistic that the husbands paying the money have incomes of more than twice as much as the mothers looking after the children. I say the mothers because the parent who is paying the maintenance in 98 per cent of the cases is the father and the other 2 per cent of course is the mother looking after the children.
That does not leave a lot of funding for the mother and children to live on. This statistic was based on the tax situation in 1988 but according to Statistics Canada very little had changed since 1988 so the problem is still there.
The study also showed that alimony and child support on average made up only 15 per cent of the income of the women who received it. That is an unfair statistic I would suggest because what we are talking about here are a large number of cases where the custodial parent
Government Orders
does not receive any maintenance whatsoever. If you average it out over all the families that are separated or divorced where one parent is looking after children and receiving maintenance from the other the income of the mother and children existing in the family is only 15 per cent.
It gives you an idea of how serious the situation is in our communities. What we are talking about are the children of Canada, a large number of children. It is certainly not the majority of children, but a very large number have become children at risk through the system and its neglect or its insufficient attention. These children will be the citizens of tomorrow. We are not guarding this resource. Not only are we not guarding it we are in many cases abandoning its welfare.
We have heard more and more of the situation that exists with respect to crime in our communities. Now more than ever we are concentrating on crime prevention and the reduction of violence in our communities.
While we are concentrating on this and talking about longer sentences for offenders, while we are talking about retribution, more and more evidence is coming forward that we need rehabilitation, treatment and care for the young people in our society.
One psychiatrist testified before the Standing Committee on Justice which studied the question of crime prevention. This psychiatrist is very knowledgeable in crime prevention and children at risk, the very young people in our community. He testified that the most important age for assistance as far as the reduction of crime is concerned, where our dollar can have the greatest impact in reducing crime, is between the time the child is bom and the child's third or fourth birthday.
Now that is quite a significant statement. It shows that the younger the child is the more of an impact we can have in bringing that child forward as a citizen who does not resent his or her treatment in society and who does not represent a child at risk who could become a potential violator of the laws in this country.
It has also been said by many and the statistic that sticks in my mind is that for every dollar we put into the welfare of a child below the age of seven we will save $7 in reduced cost to the community in incarceration, rehabilitation, court costs and police costs. Investing $1 will save $7 if we want to look after our very young people.

February 12, 1993
Government Orders
However, we are not doing it. We are not doing it because of the stereotypical, preconceived attitudes that have existed in this country for some time. We are not doing it because we do not want to change. We want to tinker with the system a little but we really do not want to change it.
We are not changing it even though many women, because of the low maintenance and low support they receive for themselves and their children, have to supplement their income. Two-thirds of the women who receive alimony and child support are raising their children by themselves.
They are left with this very important-I do not want to say difficult because difficult is not the word, although raising a family is not easy today. Important is the best word because they are raising and moulding the citizens who will be in charge of this country tomorrow.
In that there is this important role, this important and meaningful procedure and this important and meaningful task ahead. We all should be supporting these women, these partners of broken marriages who are looking after our children.
What is the reality? The reality is that the majority of Canadian child support orders are in arrears. The majority are in arrears. Most mother-led post-divorce families live in poverty. That is over 50 per cent. This would still be the case even if all payments were made. That remark comes from no source less than the Department of Justice. The reason that even if all maintenance payments were made over 50 per cent of the mother-led post-divorce families live in poverty because the support payments are ridiculously low. Two-thirds live in poverty. That is, with payments being made two-thirds live in poverty. If the payments are not made, 75 per cent of mother-children households would live in poverty.
The Ontario government, as the parliamentary secretary has said, has taken over the collection of support payments in the province of Ontario. I join with him in congratulating it on that. This is important because the stalling and the deflection that has gone on in enforcing these payments has been totally tragic. It has been a national tragedy in Canada. But even with the full support of the Government of Ontario, and I think it is
sincere in this, in that province 75 per cent of maintenance orders are in arrears. Goodness knows what the situation would be if it was not supporting them.
Research by Miriam Grassby published in May 1991 in Reports of Family Law shows that the average support awarded is considerably less than half of the actual cost of raising a child.
Therefore, in a family where maintenance payments are received, less than half of the needs of the child in that mother-led family are met by the support payments. That is just for the necessities. That is absolutely no money for the mother for leisure activities or for any kind of retirement package. That is unheard of. There is no retirement package, nothing that could be put aside. Just forget about that completely. The mother is supposed to completely forget about any kind of recreation, any kind of free time, any kind of pleasure or leisure activities or any kind of money put aside for retirement or whatever.
The case seems to be that it is hard to deny your children if you are living with them, but it is easy if you are not. I am not condemning the former husbands. This is not an easy situation. This is not cut and dried. When there is a divorce and a breakup of the family, there is a tremendous amount of animosity.
Sometimes the mother is resentful and if she has custody of the children she does not want the father to have access. If the father does have access, or the court says the father is to have access, she may throw roadblocks in the father's way. The father may be well-meaning at the beginning but because of the frustration and aggravation of trying to see the children he finally says he is not going to go through the hassle and is not going to bother trying to gain access to the children.
That is one way of doing it. That is understandable, with the degree of aggravation, but that is not fulfilling the role for the children. You may dislike your former wife intensely but the fact of the matter is the children are so very important. We cannot just look at the animosity that exists between two adults who are not putting the welfare of the children first and foremost, or one who is and one who is not, it does not matter which one. I do not want to get into that kind of an appraisal this afternoon.

It is sufficient to say that more consideration must be given to the children. As well, judges seem to be unaware of the barriers to a woman becoming self-sufficient if she is older, say in her forties. Not only may she be lacking in skills, experience and opportunity but as the custodial parent she is not free to travel, to work long hours, study at night or socialize with colleagues and may not be able to hold employment, a job that she wants to hold.
That is in addition to the fact that sometimes in marriage the wife sacrifices her career for the husband's career. She does not follow through with her own career because she is working with the children, helping them and moulding these citizens of tomorrow.
The husband can carry on and he does. The divorce takes place. The husband carries on with his career but the wife has jettisoned her career. She does not have a career. She tries to pick it up but she also must care for the children. She also must find a job. As a result of the fact that she has given up these important years of work and does not have the experience but does have an increased age she becomes less and less marketable as a prospective employee.
Add to that the inequities of the tax system. In our tax system a man gets to deduct his child support payments directly from the amount of tax he must pay. If a maintenance order is awarded by the court, if the court says to the estranged husband who is living apart from his former wife and children that he must pay so many dollars a month for the support of his children the husband is not taxed on that amount but it is considered as revenue to the mother. Not only are the courts awarding less than what is necessary for the support of the children but what the mother receives for supporting herself and primarily the children is taxable. She gets even less than what is awarded in dollar terms.
The federal government actually subsidizes the lifestyle of the divorced man to a large extent. There are many divorced men who are faithful in making these payments. They are good fathers who go out of their way to keep in contact with their children. These men really deserve an amount of credit that is not being given to them.
Government Orders
That father has affection for the children. It is difficult when the mother gets custody of the children and the father does not get to keep contact but must pay. He is obviously a man who is putting the consideration of the children first. That is really vital, and he knows that.
Quite often he is paying more than he feels he should be paying, and in many cases he is right. He is paying, he is being taken advantage of. There are lots of ways in which that can be done. It is not one-sided. It is a complicated situation. It is not cut and dried.
In 1988 men deducted $1.3 billion from their income tax for child support payments and saved themselves $475 million in taxes. The government then collected about $275 million in taxes from the recipients of the support payments. That leaves what we could call a divorce subsidy of approximately $200 million. That $275 million, although lower than what the husbands would have paid, was really grinding down the single mothers with children who had to pay that amount of taxes.
Advocates of the system say that it encourages judges to award larger support payments if the husbands do not have to pay taxes. It is also said that many husbands are married a second time and have second families and that there is only so much they can contribute. That is an argument, but there is absolutely no proof whatsoever that husbands separated or divorced from their families are encouraged to pay maintenance or alimony by the mere fact that they do not have to pay taxes on that amount.
Why should husbands and fathers feel that they do not have an obligation? Why should anyone have to be encouraged to support their children, whether they are children living in the family home or children and mothers living outside the family home?
An Ontario government report presented in November 1992 said that child support payments should not be deductible or included in the calculation of taxable income. There should be no tax ramifications at all for maintenance payments or alimony payments. It should be treated as income by the husband and passed along to the former wife and children without any tax ramifications or tax payable by the former wife at all.

February 12, 1993
Government Orders
That is a recent recommendation by the Government of Ontario. It acknowledges in this study that to do so may cause some courts to re-examine the maintenance orders by arguing that if the husband has to pay taxes then that is more of an outlay by him, and therefore they will have to reduce the orders.
In order to stop the onslaught of realignments of maintenance payments or re-examination of maintenance payments the report states that the taxes payable by the former husband should be phased in each year. For example, each year over a five or ten-year period the husband should pay a higher percentage of taxes until the final result would be that there would be no tax ramifications. It would be treated as income to the estranged husband and no taxes will be paid by the former wife and mother who is looking after the children. The parliamentary secretary mentioned that.
The present situation is costing taxpayers $235 million a year. The 1990 taxation statistics reveal that not only are divorced fathers and husbands being given a tax break but an additional $66 million is not being claimed by the estranged wives and mothers who have the custody of the children. The mothers are in such a difficult financial situation that they try to dodge the tax payments. Through what they consider to be absolute necessity they try to avoid payment of the taxes they should be paying by not declaring their support payments. It is a fact that the government is losing $66 million in that way.
The present tax deduction that men receive when they pay support is arrived at by rewarding the payer for meeting his obligations. That is not something of which there is any proof. There is no substantiation for that case.
The amount of support to be paid should be more in keeping with what is necessary. Whether it is a reality that the courts must face, or whether it is a tax change, there must be change to reflect the need for single mothers with children estranged from former husbands to have more support.
It is also in the interest of the community to ensure that this happens because the children of today are the citizens of tomorrow. They must be considered. They have to be considered because if we do not consider them then we are asking for a great deal of trouble in the future. We cannot forget about the children of this country without paying the price.
In addition to the problems that women face, quite often what they receive is what the lawyer wants. There may not be maintenance payments over a period of time. There may be a lump sum payment. That may be what the lawyer will advocate and not only advocate but absolutely demand. The lawyer may actually take his or her client to court to get what the lawyer feels is in his or her interest in terms of legal fees.
There could be $10,000 awarded to the mother for herself and the children without any maintenance payments over a period of time. That whole $10,000, and perhaps even more, could be taken by the lawyer. That leaves the mother and the children without anything as a result of the divorce settlement.
I once again congratulate the province of Ontario for trying to do something, at least in the initial stages, to correct men's ability to stall. The longer husbands work at trying to stall their maintenance payments the better they become because they know a little about the law. They get to know a little more about the system. They know that perhaps the system will not enforce the orders.
Perhaps they are big movers and shakers in the community and have some clout and that helps them to stall their maintenance payments. That helps them to renege on the support for their children and their former wife. They get to know it a little more as time goes along and of course their lawyers are a big help to them in that regard. That is not to criticize lawyers. Lawyers are there to help their clients and there are good clients and bad clients-
Good lawyers and bad lawyers.

There are good lawyers and bad lawyers. That is one of the problems.
The other problem is that maintenance orders are not being enforced. They can be held up for years. What does a family do in the meantime? The father can also use the Divorce Act to have payments reassessed and there are various ways of delaying the actual maintenance payments themselves.
Maybe there should be mandatory interest charges and penalties on overdue payments. Possibly that is one way of demonstrating that society is not going to tolerate the neglect of children in the various communities. Maybe, and I say more than maybe, there should be more negotiations in the federal-provincial area to deal with this situation. The actual collection and enforcement of
February 12, 1993

maintenance orders falls within provincial jurisdiction. One of the problems we have in our great country is that divorce is a federal statute but the enforcement of maintenance payments is provincial. Therefore, some areas are in federal jurisdiction and some in provincial.
The parliamentary secretary has stated that there is some movement, some negotiations between the Minister of Justice and his counterparts in the provinces. I want to say that if movement is there it must be measured with a microscope because there is very little evidence of any movement. In fact, in 1992 there were two federal-provincial conferences on justice planned with the attorneys general and both were cancelled by the Minister of Justice.
In fairness, there was the referendum and a few other things that came about, but the fact is that priority was not given to what the government says it feels very strongly about. It was not given at all. There was no priority given to deal with this.
The new Minister of Justice says there will be a symposium from March 10 to 12, where federal-provincial problems will be dealt with. They will deal with young offenders, the problems of maintenance payments, crime prevention and many other areas where federal-provincial negotiations must take place.
It will be a two and a half day conference. How in the name of heaven are any conclusions going to be arrived at? How are we possibly going to reach any kind of improvement in two and a half days with federal, provincial, municipal officials and officials from all the organizations that deal with crime prevention in Canada at the conference in Toronto? It is absolutely incredible that we should be expected to believe there is going to be progress. There is no progress now and there is no indication that the federal government wants to make progress in addressing this tremendously important area.
The fact of the matter is that we are in the last century in the way we deal with this question. Even when the courts talk about support and funding for estranged mothers and children or the former wife and mother, they talk about the major asset as being real property, the family home or whatever property they have, be it real or personal. They do not talk about the main
Government Orders
financial area as being the earning power of the father which is the main area which has to be considered.
We seem to be going around in circles on this question. We seem to be taking three steps forward and two back. If this country is going to work it has to be meaningful for the people who live in this country. It has to be meaningful for Canadians. It has to be meaningful for the needs of the future, and the needs of the future are our children. We are doing a tremendous injustice both to the children and our future.
If we do not come to grips with this, if we cannot get the federal government and the provinces to come together to deal with this very important question of maintenance of the mother and the children, if we cannot provide meaningful assistance, if we must say that these children and single parents must live without the maintenance orders to which they are entitled and they have been awarded by the courts of this country, if we have to say that the Canadian public has to pick it up in any fashion possible, perhaps by welfare payments or by charity, then what are we saying? We are saying that this country does not work. We are saying that the future is not important. We are saying that the children of this country can be left to fend for themselves. We are saying that we are not serious about crime prevention. We are saying that we just do not care.
I want it to be known by all Canadians that that is what they are saying. I want everyone to know that that is what they are saying so it does not become a shock, a surprise and a rude awakening to this country as the years go along. I want them to know. I want them to have the chance to do something about it.
This government knows that it does not care. This government knows that it is not going to do anything. It is not putting themselves out for the children of this country and our leaders of tomorrow. It has made its choice and that choice is to do very little. That is not good enough. It is not good enough for this side of the House and I know it is not good enough for most Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to follow my colleague from Cape Breton who spoke forcefully and clearly on many of the issues that are raised in this discussion of family law reform brought forward by Bill C-79.

February 12, 1993
Government Orders
I would like to say before going into any of the technical aspects of the bill and the function that it performs that some of the issues which are touched on by revisions to the support for families in the event of divorce go beyond the narrow scope of that issue.
Bill C-79 provides an opportunity for this House to consider many of the things that concern our electors, the citizens of Canada, about the developments in modem society. Some of them relate to divorce and support for dependent spouses and children in the event of divorce but I think others relate to the fundamental issue of how well Canada is doing in the context of providing for its weakest and its poorest.
We all know and we all shared a great deal of pride in the fact that according to some standards the United Nations indicated last year that Canada had the best standard of living in the world. This reflects a number of aspects of Canadian society of which we are all justifiably proud.
What I think those of us who are concerned especially at this time and what we are aware of is the fact that despite the excellent quality of life, despite the fact that Canadians enjoy great opportunity, great freedom we also have within our borders an undue level of poverty. We have too many children, we have too many adults, who face very grim prospects as we go into a continuing winter of recession.
Unemployment remains high, in excess of 11 per cent. There are 1.5 million Canadians out of work. Poverty is clearly related to unemployment. The problems we face in our cities, in our rural areas are continually reflective of the level of poverty that has been increasing sadly over the past few years.
The 1980s were the first decade since the Second World War in which real family income failed to grow over the course of that decade. This reflects a number of things. In particular, it reflects the fact that government charges have been increasing at a very rapid rate through all of that time. Government charges in the form of taxes at both income tax levels as well as property taxes or wealth taxes, which have increased dramatically in many municipalities across the country, have imposed a greater burden on families. At the same time, real incomes
were not increasing as rapidly as inflation was occurring during that decade.
It reflects the fact that our economy has gone through a period of difficult restructuring. There have been a lot of high paying jobs lost permanently during the course of that decade and the early years of the 1990s.
To some extent it is fair to say that the policies pursued by the government have contributed over the last three years directly to the degree and intensity of the recession that we face. We all know that the Governor of the Bank of Canada pursued a policy of what he called price stability, some called it zero inflation, with great ardour and intensity. His objective was more or less achieved but at a price of many jobs being lost.
It is interesting when you look at the pursuit of that policy by the Bank of Canada to always remember that the bank pursues monetary policy with the consent and agreement of the government. The Minister of Finance meets on a regular basis with the Governor of the Bank of Canada. He has the power to tell the governor to pursue a different policy. The policy we are talking about is the government's policy.
That policy to drive inflation out of the system was pursued at the same time as the government was implementing a free trade agreement with the United States. The perversity of doing those two things at the same time is demonstrated by the fact that the Canadian dollar which traded at 76 cents U.S. in October 1987 when the free trade agreement was signed, reached a peak of 89 cents in November 1991.
Meanwhile we lead the U.S. into recession. We suffered extremely high levels of unemployment, much higher that those in the United States. The result for our people has been a continuing round of poverty which remains unabated to this point in time.
It is clear that where unemployment is a problem, where the economy is weak, the price is paid by families first. It is clear that where financial problems arise, the problems within families increase.
The difficulty of dealing with the stress that is imposed by financial hardship is a clear, frequent contributor to the breakdown of marriages and is, in a direct way, a contributor to the problems we are trying to deal with in
February 12, 1993

part with this bill when we are dealing with support for estranged spouses and dependant children.
It is impossible to simply take the objective of this bill, which is a worthy one which we are supporting, and deal with it apart from the over-all economic situation the country is in. To ignore the consequences of the economic policies of this government and simply applaud the fact that it is doing more to ensure that child support can be collected, is to ignore the really important factor, the failure of this government's economic policies which has led directly to the breakdown of many families and has caused hardship and poverty in families across the country.
The reality is that the majority of child support orders in Canada is in arrears. I dare say that many of those arrears are caused by the fact that the supporting parent has become unemployed and is unable to earn a living.
Even if all of the payments were made, it seems that most mother led post-divorced families would still be living in poverty.
In this country, surely one of the most prosperous in the history of the world, we continue to see in our cities and in our rural areas cases of poverty, cases of hunger. It is a disgrace and all of us should be ashamed.
Over the last few years I have had the privilege within my own region of Ottawa-Carle ton and in Ottawa South of working with the Ottawa food bank and with UNICEF every year to try to address the issues of hunger in our community, which are addressed in part by the food bank and in the broader international community in which UNICEF plays a part.
Each year we encourage people to spend 24 hours without food in order that they may understand to some extent the nature of hunger when it really strikes. It is very short-lived. It is not something that necessarily changes a person's life, but it is a realization of the fact that hunger is one of those things that is part of the human experience. Very few of us in this House have experienced it in any real and enduring way but it is a fact of life for millions of Canadians.
Government Orders
Until we begin to see the economy expanding again and people getting back to work, sadly hunger and poverty will increase rather than decline in our land.
As well, it is clear that poverty and hunger have a direct relationship to the ability of children to perform in educational facilities. Throughout Canada school-boards, especially in the large cities, are instituting breakfast programs and other food programs to ensure that students have enough to eat. They cannot work in their classrooms if they are hungiy.
All these issues are tied together. It is not possible to take them apart and deal with them on a segmented basis. We need to understand the nature of the over-all problem if we are to begin to address it.
With respect to the payments of child support, what has to be understood is that again and again our judicial system has failed, usually because of complexity, to make it easier for dependent spouses to collect support payments. This has contributed to the futility of lives, the futility of people trying to find ways to keep their families together, to keep them from being completely tom apart by the lack of resources.
According to some research published in the May 1991 issue of the Reports of Family Law by Miriam Grassby, the average support awarded is considerably less than half the actual cost of raising a child. According to the research paper this means that an already impoverished wife ends up paying a disproportionate share of child costs. She is left with no money for leisure or savings, or even for a modest retirement. She ends up footing the bill for the emotional and recreational needs of her children, needs that an absent ex-husband can easily ignore.
According to Miss Grassby, and I quote: "It is easy to deprive children if you appear to be paying a large amount for child support. It is veiy difficult to deprive children if you are living with them".
This points out a very important factor in the way we deal with these issues in our society. Sometimes I think that when we passed the Charter of Rights and Freedoms we ought to have called it the charter of rights and responsibilities. Maybe there is still room in Canada for us to enact a charter of responsibilities.

February 12, 1993
Government Orders
Based on the evidence that exists of the occurrence of poverty in mother-led, post-divorce families in Canada, it is clear that there are fathers across this land who do not consider their responsibilities to their former wives and to their children to be important enough to ensure that they do not live in poverty.
It was said, I think by Franklin Roosevelt, that we cannot prepare the future for our youth but we can prepare our youth for the future. If we allow this problem to continue, if we fail to address the needs of the children living in Canada in poverty today, we will have to deal with the problems that creates in the future. They are the people upon whom we are going to depend for the future of our country. They need to be supported and prepared for that today.
The situation that befalls a mother-led family after a divorce is often a difficult and grim one. Frequently we find the mother is ill-prepared to become the economic support for the family unit. The pressures of raising children even in a traditional family unit are significant. I can say from experience that there is a lot to taking care of a family with children.
A mother-led family that is without adequate support from a former spouse finds it difficult to collect support without going to see lawyers and paying the legal fees or trying to negotiate with Legal Aid to get assistance to pursue a husband that is not paying support payments.
It is difficult to find housing in many of our cities where vacancy rates are extremely low and where affordable housing is difficult to find. The training and experience of a mother who has been out of the work force for a period of years make it difficult for her to re-enter the labour force, to find a job that pays adequately. There are pressures to accommodate the needs of children whatever they may be. Whatever their interests or involvements may be they cost a lot. It costs a lot to have a 10-year-old in minor hockey. Yet, if our children are to have the opportunity to enjoy the lives that we hope for them, these costs have to be taken into account.
We think we have a free, publicly funded education system in this country. Anyone with children in the public education system knows very well it is not free. We know very well the requests for special payments to go on field trips, to buy books, to join the clubs and to
play in the volleyball tournaments. All these things cost a lot of money.
What parent, however difficult their circumstances are, wants to be the one to say to their children: "No, you cannot be part of that team. No, you cannot engage in that activity. No, you cannot go on that field trip because I cannot afford it". What parent wants to go to the school and say: "Please, I would like to apply for the subsidy so that my child can go on the field trip. Because my support payment has not come in this month I cannot afford to do it".
This is the reality of living in our modem society in Canada. It looks very good from some points of view, so good that we can be considered to have the best standard of living in the world in some quarters, and yet for others who are deprived of sharing in that it can be very difficult.
I want to talk a bit about the issue with respect to the tax system raised by the parliamentary secretary and my colleague from Cape Breton. The numbers according to the 1988 statistics were interesting. They indicated that in 1988 supporting husbands deducted $1.3 billion in child support from their income tax. Therefore they saved $475 million in taxes. The receiving spouses in turn declared the support payments and paid about $275 million in taxes on them. In other words the difference of about $200 million in lost tax revenue is considered by some to be a subsidy for divorce; the government subsidizes divorce to the extent of $200 million.
If the $200 million were going to dependent spouses we may be able to say it is justifiable, that it makes it available. However the reality is that $200 million is staying with the paying spouses.
Would it not be better to look at readjustment of the system so that the $200 million goes directly to meeting the needs of the families, to looking after the problem of child care and the problem faced by many mother-led families of getting new training and experience to find jobs. These are the needs of these mother-led families. That is where the problem arises, and that is where we need to be adjusting the focus of our attention.
For that matter, again by imposing the tax burden on receiving spouses we add to the difficulties mother-led families often have in completing tax returns, in making proper claims and in knowing the records are correct.
February 12, 1993

These difficulties could simply be avoided by adjusting the system so that the obligation to pay tax was shifted.
All these points underline the fact that the women of Canada are and have been most hit by divorce. I would like to leave this statistic with the House: men who paid alimony and child support had incomes that were more than double those of women they sent the money to, according to a study released last year by Statistics Canada. This points out the fact that usually the women who have children in their care suffer the most by divorce.
Our support for Bill C-79 indicates our concern that the collection procedures be simplified so that support payments that are ordered are actually collected. It is the sadness that results from the economic policies of this government that must not be overlooked in considering the poverty in which many of these people live.

Madam Speaker, I will be picking up on some of the themes that have just been spoken to by colleagues on this side of the House.
We support Bill C-79 in principle but certainly the analogy of using a band-aid for a serious disease would apply to this bill. I quickly read through the bill and it was difficult to find anything that any person of good will would disagree with.
The government just does not get it. As on so many issues it does not get the fact that separated and divorced mothers and children have bigger problems. This will do some good, but if this is the best this government that is about to be voted out of office can do, after eight years, why did it not do this years ago? Why did it not do so much years ago? Why did it mandate the Governor of the Bank of Canada to come down on less fortunate Canadians, often single mothers, disproportionately single mothers? Why did it mandate the Governor of the Bank of Canada to make fighting inflation his only goal? At what price have they won that battle? How many single mothers have lost a job working for the federal government, working for a federal Crown corporation, working in the private sector, so that a few thousand Canadians living at the top of Westmount, in Forest Hill Village and the like can live better than they did eight
Government Orders
years ago? Some of them are not living so well these days either I understand.
What we have learned is that we need a government that tries to represent all Canadians, not just the wealthy few thousand in a few cities in our country. That is why this government is going to get itself-I do not think it is going to be surprised-a real lesson when people go to vote at the upcoming election.
To speak more directly to the bill, as you heard earlier, Madam Speaker, the majority of Canadian child support orders are in arrears I understand. Most mother-led, post-divorce families live in poverty, but that would be the case even if all of the payments were being made, because the orders themselves are ridiculously low.
Our judges still need to be sensitized. At least in my province they are getting better but they still have not got it yet. I am sure they have to be sensitized in other communities. I am told by a friend who recently became divorced that they need to be sensitized in the Ottawa-Hull area to the issues of what is an adequate payment to a wife and children.
Without those payments made pursuant to a separation or divorce order, 75 per cent of mother-children households live in poverty. The Ontario government, as I think we heard earlier, has now taken over the collection of support payments, 75 per cent of which are now in arrears. We heard reference earlier by my colleague from Ottawa South and I believe my colleague from Cape Breton to Miriam Grassby and I will not take up time on that.
I believe too many judges across the country seem to be unaware of the barriers to a woman becoming self-sufficient. She is older, perhaps in her forties. Not only might she be lacking in work skills outside the family, and experience, but as the custodial parent she is not free to travel, work long hours, study at night and that sort of thing.
This brings me to the income tax issue. Again, I am advised that we cannot amend this bill to amend the Income Tax Act with respect to child support payments. I hope I can convince you in a moment, Madam Speaker, this is a very major problem.
The custodial parent, virtually always the former wife, pays tax on child support as if it was her income. Child support payments are not income of course but a

February 12, 1993
Government Orders
spouse's contribution to raising children. Most European countries, the United States and Australia do not tax child support payments in the hands of the mother. Why do we in this country?
Non-custodial parents claim a substantial tax deduction. The figure was given by my colleague from Ottawa South a moment ago that two-thirds of divorced mothers and their children receiving support live below the poverty line.
We have, I am proud to say, in Edmonton an organization called "People Against Child Support Taxation", PACT which has launched a campaign to throw out the law which taxes child support payments.
I have written to the Minister of Finance and I will refer to what his views on that matter are in a moment. It is essential that single parents receiving child support that is taxed join in the battle for a fairer tax system that will reflect the real needs of single parents and their children. I hope anyone watching today in that position will feel urged to contact, in most cases, her member of Parliament.
I have a couple of further comments. The custodial parent pays tax on the child support as if it were income. It is not income, as I said. This money is reimbursement for living expenses involved in raising children. Two-thirds of divorced mothers and their children receiving support live below the poverty line. Susan Thibaudeau, a social worker in Quebec, as members will know, has filed a class action lawsuit on behalf of 300 women challenging this tax provision.
For the last three years Madam Thibaudeau to her great credit has been filing separate tax returns for her children claiming child support as their income. When filing this way you are subject to interest in penalties but she feels-I am sure you are aware of this Madam Speaker being from Quebec-that it is worth it for such children when they look at the long-term consequences of being overtaxed.
I might also add that women suffer as a result of this extra so-called income in terms of decreased eligibility for student loans, for subsidized day care and subsidized housing. The burden is on women going through divorce to prepare statements on the before and after tax impact of receiving child support.
This brings me to a letter I wrote in June to the Minister of Finance, the member for Vegreville. I refer to a couple of things that have already been mentioned. I wrote first:
Once a court divorce order is issued, the spouse with more than half the custody for the children (virtually always the former wife) must pay income tax on the other's support payments whereas the other can deduct such payments from his taxable income. In recent years, approximately 264,000 women across Canada have paid taxes on such support.
The practical effects of this almost unique Canadian practice in effect since the 1940s-

-France appears to be the only other industrial democracy to follow us in this dreadful practice,

-are very serious. For example, one of my visitors-
I was referring to people who had come to see me.
-pointed out that fully $385 of the $800 she receives monthly must be put aside for taxes.
Of course, she is one of the lucky ones to get $800 a month. How many separated wives get $800 a month from their former spouses?
This leaves her constantly attempting to keep the financial noses of her children and herself above water. Approximately two-thirds of divorced women and children live below the poverty line-whereas only 16 per cent of divorced men are below the poverty line after paying child support.
In 1988, men deducted about $1.2 billion in support payments, thus saving $475 million in taxes. Government then collected about $275 million in taxes from those receiving support, thereby providing a divorce subsidy of about $200 million.
Imagine at the end of the 20th century a so-called government of an industrialized democracy subsidizing divorce. Where are the members of the government caucus on this issue?
The answer to those who assert that not allowing ex-husbands to deduct their payments would increase the numbers of defaulters is that the default rates in both Canada and the U.S. (where deductions are not allowed) is about the same.
It is 75 per cent I am sorry to say.
I wrote to the minister that it would strike any fan-minded government or person that the tax system:
-concedes about $ 12 billion yearly for RRSPs and $ 2.6 billion for capital gains exemptions yet encourages most single mothers to live in grinding poverty shrieks for reform.
February 12, 1993

Here is what our wonderful Minister of Finance, this great humanitarian replied on August 31. He explained the system. I think my letter made it clear that his reply would be made public so I do not think I am breaching any confidence by quoting from his letter. He said:
On the other hand, the disposable income of a recipient of child support payments is increased by reason of the amount received. As you can also appreciate, a child support payment received is disposable income in the same manner as income earned in employment and is appropriately taxable as an income source. It would be unfair, for example, to make child support payments tax exempt while imposing tax on employment income earned by a single mother to support her child.
It goes on further and if you can imagine, it gets even worse:
It should also be noted that the Courts and the legal practitioners are well aware of the tax status of child support payments and the amount of court ordered or negotiated payments reflect these tax results. Indeed, as a result of the deductibility of these payments, larger maintenance amounts are encouraged.
If I have not convinced you yet, Madam Speaker, I will quote the Minister of Finance of our great country writing this kind of stuff:
With regard to the status of single parents, the government's assistance to families with children is being restructured as outlined in my February 25, 1992 budget.
I will stop there.
